title: Galaxy NGC 2397 with an explosive secret
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 2397, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 2397 · constellation Volans · about 60 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA & Stephen Smartt (Queen's University Belfast, UK)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Long, prominent dust lanes run along the edges of the spiral arms of NGC 2397 in this Hubble image, showing as dark patches and streaks against the glow of starlight. It is a classic spiral galaxy, lying nearly 60 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Volans.

In many ways NGC 2397 is typical of spirals. Its central portion is dominated by older, yellow and red stars, while star formation carries on in its outer, bluer spiral arms. Young stars tend to be hot and blue, so the color of a region hints at the age of the stars within it.

Hubble's sharp resolution makes it possible to study individual stars in nearby galaxies. With the Advanced Camera for Surveys, the brightest of the young, blue stars in the arms can be picked out one by one, rather than blurring together into a general glow.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.53 x 2.02 arcminutes) and distance (60 million light years), the frame spans roughly 44,000 × 35,000 light-years. Its light set out about 60 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: No eye could pick out individual stars in a galaxy this far away, and part of the data is near-infrared light we cannot see.
